stories.h2: The light bulb was only the beginning.
stories.lead: On the afternoon of 4 September 1882, about 400 electric lamps came on in lower Manhattan. A practical lamp had existed for almost three years. What took so long was everything around it: dynamos, miles of underground copper, fuses, meters, switches, factories, a franchise from the city — and a price that could compete with gas.
stories.sub: The story usually told is about a filament. The more useful one is about a system — and how many people, in how many countries, it took to build.
stories.caption: The Pearl Street dynamo room, 1882 · painted illustration

stories.h2: From computational biology to a business built on science.
stories.lead: In 2000, a group of Bangalore computer scientists bet that the mathematics of algorithms could help make sense of biology. Turning that bet into a company meant software, a global partnership, a wet lab and external accreditation — each a different business around the same science.
stories.sub: Strand Life Sciences, and what it takes for research capability to become a sustainable enterprise.
stories.caption: Computational biology in Bangalore · painted illustration

stories.h2: GPS became much more than a way to find your location.
stories.lead: The most important thing a GPS satellite broadcasts is not a location. It is the time. Built for the military, GPS became a free public clock and coordinate system — and an economy grew on top of it that its designers never planned.
stories.sub: How public research becomes a platform that thousands of others build on.
stories.caption: A navigation satellite above India · painted illustration
